Corot based his large oil painting on drawings and oil sketches made outdoors. Attracted to the beauty of the Italian countryside, he often sketched around Rome, where he lived from 1825 to 1828. This painting's highly structured composition, based on forms moving into the distance along a series of diagonals, is characteristic of Corot's early style and recalls the classical landscapes of 17th-century painter Nicholas Poussin.

source_title: Mule Entering Barn Mechanical Coin Bank
desc_src: Cast iron mechanical bank depicting a mule, dog and barn.To make a deposit, a coin is placed between the mule's hind legs; pushing the lever will cause the mule to kick its legs and transfer the coin into the barn. At the same time, the dog will emerge from the barn. Manufactured by the J and E Stevens Company circa 1880. Title: Mule Entering Barn Mechanical Coin Bank

source_title: Low Waterfall in a Wooded Landscape with a Dead Beech Tree
desc_src: Jutting from a dune in the foreground, the massive silvery trunk of a dead tree leads the eye across a waterfall and toward a distant sunlit field where travelers and a dog traverse a sandy path. Partly masked by trees, a ruined building is turned gold by the sun. In Jacob van Ruisdael’s landscapes, dead trees, waterfalls, and ruined buildings were visual expressions of the passage of time. Ruisdael devoted equal attention to the cloud-filled skies looming above the land, creating dramatic patterns of light and shadow and revealing the unseen movements of the wind.

source_title: Boys Stealing Watermelons Mechanical Coin Bank
desc_src: Cast iron mechanical bank. Depicts two African American boys stealing watermelons from a field guarded by a dog in a doghouse. To make a deposit, a coin is placed in the slot on top of the dog house. Pushing a lever moves the dog out of the house allowing the coin to fall. The action also animates the boys' arms. Manufactured by the Kyser and Rex Company from 1885 to 1895. Title: Boys Stealing Watermelons Mechanical Coin Bank
